t.4.19.1: That great king of the monkeys, lying wounded by the arrow, having been answered with words full of reason, offered no reply.
t.4.19.2: His limbs shattered by rocks, violently struck by trees, and overcome by Rāma's arrow, he swooned at the end of his life.
t.4.19.3: Tārā heard that Vālin, that tiger among monkeys, had been slain in battle by the release of an arrow, dealt by Rāma on account of a wife.
t.4.19.5: But those mighty vānaras who formed Aṅgada's retinue, seeing Rāma with his bow, fled in terror.
t.4.19.4: Having heard the unwelcome news of her husband's most dreadful slaying, she, together with her son, rushed out of the many-chambered mountain cavern, the two of them sorely frightened.
t.4.19.6: Then she saw the terrified monkeys rushing swiftly toward her, like deer that have strayed from their herd after the leader of the herd has been slain.
t.4.19.7: Approaching them, she, herself grieving, spoke, O Rāma, to all of them, who were grieving and terrified, as if pursued by arrows.
t.4.19.8: O monkeys, you who marched before that lion among kings, why do you abandon him and flee, wretched and terrified?
t.4.19.10: Having heard the words of the monkey-king's wife, the monkeys, who could take any form at will, spoke to that woman words that were timely and coherent.
t.4.19.9: If, for the sake of the kingdom, that brother, a brother indeed, has been cruelly struck down by Rāma with far-flying arrows loosed from a distance…
t.4.19.11: O mother of a living son, turn back and protect your son Aṅgada! Death, in the form of Rāma, has slain Vālin and is carrying him away.
t.4.19.12: Having shattered the trees that were hurled, and the huge rocks as well, he felled Vālī with arrows like thunderbolts, as though Vālī were struck down by the thunderbolt itself.
t.4.19.13: This entire army, set upon, has fled and scattered in all directions, now that this tiger among monkeys, whose splendor equaled Śakra's, has been slain.
t.4.19.14: Let the city be guarded by heroes, and let Aṅgada be consecrated as king; the monkeys will serve Vālin's son once he is established in his father's place.
t.4.19.15: Or else, O lovely-faced one, a pleasing place is yours right here, for the vānaras are swiftly entering their strongholds this very day.
t.4.19.16: Here dwell forest-rangers, some without wives and some with wives; from our own kinsmen, covetous and deprived, there is great and tumultuous fear for us.
t.4.19.17: Having heard the words of those who had gone only a short distance away, that sweetly smiling woman spoke in a manner worthy of herself.
t.4.19.18: What use have I for my son, what for the kingdom, what for my own self, when that illustrious lion among monkeys, my husband, is perishing?
t.4.19.19: I shall go to the very feet of that great-souled one, he who lies there struck down by the arrow loosed by Rāma.
t.4.19.20: Having spoken thus, she ran forth weeping, wasted by grief, beating her head and breast with both her arms in her anguish.
t.4.19.21: Then, as she approached, she saw her husband fallen upon the ground, he who had slain the lords of the Dānavas, those who never turned back in battle.
t.4.19.22: Him who hurled the lords of mountains as Vāsava hurls his thunderbolts, who was filled with the force of a mighty gale, and whose roar was like that of masses of great clouds.
t.4.19.23: Him whose valor equaled Śakra's, now stilled like a cloud that has ceased after pouring its rain; the fearsome one who roared among roarers, a hero felled by a hero, slain like a king of beasts struck down by a tiger for the sake of meat.
t.4.19.24: Him who had been honored by all the world, lying like a sacred caitya with its banners and its altar, torn down by Suparṇa for the sake of a serpent.
t.4.19.25: The fair lady saw Rāma, mighty with his bow, standing as he leaned upon it, and Rāma's younger brother as well, and also her husband's younger brother.
t.4.19.26: Passing beyond them, she reached her husband, who had been struck down in battle; seeing him, she was stricken with anguish and, bewildered, fell to the ground.
t.4.19.27: Rising up again as though from sleep and crying out "O noble lord!", she wept on seeing her husband bound by the cords of death.
t.4.19.28: But Sugrīva, beholding her wailing like a kurarī bird, and seeing Aṅgada arrived there, sank into grievous despair.
